title: The Six S's of Shearing Layers

zones.label: Site
zones.summary: The land, soil, climate, and legal lot that every building on it must live with.
facts: Brand treats the site as effectively eternal: buildings come and go, but the lot and its setting remain.
Soil bearing capacity, groundwater, and frost depth are site properties that drive foundation design (Chapters 9 and 10).
Property lines, setbacks, and zoning outlast any one structure, so the site constrains every later layer.
On a Minnesota site the frost line and seasonal ground movement are design inputs, not details to fix later.

zones.label: Structure
zones.summary: The foundation and load-bearing frame, the slowest-changing part of the building itself.
facts: Brand puts structural life at roughly 30 to 300 years, depending on the building and its care.
Structure is dangerous and expensive to change, so people rarely do; everything faster has to work around it.
Foundations, columns, beams, bearing walls, and floor and roof framing make up this layer (Chapters 6 through 8 and 10).
Good design leaves structure with spare capacity and regular column spacing so the faster layers can change inside it.

zones.label: Skin
zones.summary: The exterior surfaces: cladding, roofing, windows, and doors that meet weather and fashion.
facts: Brand's rule of thumb is that skin changes roughly every 20 years as technology, weather wear, and fashion move on.
Modern skin carries the enclosure control layers for rain, air, vapor, and heat (Chapters 11 through 13).
Re-cladding or replacing windows is a common skin-layer change that should not require touching the structure.
Fastening cladding to the structure so it can be replaced separately is what lets the two layers slip past each other.

zones.label: Services
zones.summary: The working guts: wiring, plumbing, ducts, sprinklers, and elevators that keep a building habitable.
facts: Brand's range for services is about 7 to 15 years before they need replacing or upgrading, far shorter than the structure.
Electrical, HVAC, plumbing, and fire protection all belong here (Chapters 14 through 16).
Services buried inside walls and floors are costly to replace, which is why accessible chases and ceiling cavities pay off.
This layer is where the electrical designer's decisions meet the building's long-term adaptability.

zones.label: Space Plan
zones.summary: The interior layout: partitions, ceilings, floors, and doors that divide the space.
facts: Brand gives a wide range: about 3 years in commercial interiors up to roughly 30 years in homes.
Tenant improvements in offices and retail are space-plan changes, and they happen far more often than structural ones.
Non-bearing partitions are easy to move; load-bearing walls are not, so know which is which before you plan a remodel.
Demountable partitions and raised floors are design strategies that make this layer cheap to rearrange.

zones.label: Stuff
zones.summary: Furniture, equipment, and belongings: the layer that changes daily and belongs to the occupants.
facts: Stuff is in constant flux, from moving a book across a desk to replacing a whole fit-out.
Its weight still matters: furniture, shelving, and equipment are the live loads the structure was sized for (Chapter 6).
Because occupants control this layer, a building that lets people rearrange freely tends to be loved and kept.
The point of the whole poster: when fast layers are trapped inside slow ones, the building tears itself apart.

quiz.question: Which layer is described as effectively eternal, outlasting every building built on it?
quiz.explanation: The land and its legal lot persist across many generations of buildings.

quiz.question: Which layer includes soil bearing, groundwater, and the frost line that decide how a foundation must be designed?
quiz.explanation: These are properties of the land itself, so they belong to the site layer.

quiz.question: Which layer is the foundation and load-bearing frame, expensive and risky to change?
quiz.explanation: Structure lasts roughly 30 to 300 years, so everything faster has to adapt around it.

quiz.question: Which layer carries the weather-facing surfaces and is roughly replaced every 20 years?
quiz.explanation: Cladding, roofing, and windows wear out and go out of fashion about every 20 years.

quiz.question: If you re-clad a building and replace its windows, which layer are you changing?
quiz.explanation: Exterior surfaces are the skin; changing them should not require touching the structure.

quiz.question: Which layer holds wiring, ducts, pipes, and sprinklers that need replacing every 7 to 15 years?
quiz.explanation: Building services wear out and become obsolete much faster than the frame around them.

quiz.question: A tenant moves out and the next one rearranges the office partitions. Which layer changed?
quiz.explanation: Interior partitions, ceilings, and layouts are the space plan, which can turn over every few years in commercial buildings.

quiz.question: Which layer is made of furniture, equipment, and belongings that change daily?
quiz.explanation: Occupants control this fastest-moving layer, but its weight still counts as live load.
